name: Pioglitazone

lead: Pioglitazone is a prescription pill for type 2 diabetes that improves insulin sensitivity. It has been generic for years.
It shows up in appearance discussion through claims about fat tissue, but no human study has tested it for cosmetic purposes.

paras: It activates PPAR-gamma receptors, mainly in fat tissue, muscle and liver, which lowers insulin resistance. Weight gain from added subcutaneous fat is a recognised effect.
The label has a boxed warning for congestive heart failure and lists edema and fractures. Bladder cancer warnings were added in 2011. It is prescription only.

lead: Pioglitazone (brand name Actos) is an oral type 2 diabetes drug in the thiazolidinedione class. It was developed by Takeda, came into medical use in 1999 and is now generic. [1][2]

It activates the PPAR-gamma receptor, which is found in fat, muscle and liver tissue, and reduces insulin resistance. [3][1] Its label carries a boxed warning for congestive heart failure, and a known effect is weight gain attributed to increased subcutaneous fat. [3][1]

Pioglitazone appears in appearance-related discussion because of claims about fat tissue and, in one forum context, topical under-eye use. No published human study has tested pioglitazone for cosmetic purposes.

paras: The US label indicates pioglitazone as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes; it is not for type 1 diabetes or ketoacidosis. [3] Research uses have included non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, where randomized trials reported effects on liver histology. [4][5][6]
No approved cosmetic use exists. No clinical studies have tested pioglitazone, topical or oral, for under-eye appearance or facial fat.

The label's boxed warning states that thiazolidinediones cause or worsen congestive heart failure in some patients; edema and fractures are also listed as warnings. [3] Wikipedia describes mild weight gain attributed to increased subcutaneous adipose tissue. [1] Bladder cancer concerns led France to withdraw the drug in 2011 and the FDA to add label warnings; a 2017 meta-analysis reportedly found no difference in bladder cancer rates. [1] A 2007 meta-analysis of randomized trials examined cardiovascular risk with pioglitazone. [7]

Pioglitazone is a PPAR-gamma agonist; it also binds the mitochondrial protein mitoNEET. [3][1] PPAR-gamma has been studied in adipose tissue biology, including a 2012 Nature study on regulatory T cells in fat. [8] It is metabolised mainly by CYP2C8 with a half-life of roughly 3 to 7 hours. [1]

No studies found of pioglitazone for appearance or cosmetic purposes. Studies in medical conditions include the PROactive cardiovascular trial in type 2 diabetes, which found no difference in its primary composite endpoint, and trials in steatohepatitis and after stroke. [4][5][6][9]
